_meta.source: JRC ASAP (Anomaly hot Spots of Agricultural Production)
_meta.notes: Current-season agricultural stress from the EC Joint Research Centre's ASAP monthly expert assessment. Latest assessment per country from the full 2016-present series; most recent date in this run 2026-08-11. hotspot_code: 0 no hotspot, 1 hotspot, 2 major hotspot. ASAP's raw hs_code 3 means NOT ASSESSED, not a severity above 2 — those countries (8 in this run) carry hotspot_code null and stress_score null. NULL IS NOT ZERO: no assessment is not an all-clear, and several unassessed countries have dozens of subnational crop warnings standing (units_crop_warning is populated regardless of code). stress_score 0-100 is banded by the JRC verdict (0-20 / 40-70 / 75-100 for codes 0/1/2) and spread within band by units_crop_warning normalised against that country's own historical maximum — so the expert verdict always dominates the ranking and the count only breaks ties. COVERAGE IS NOT GLOBAL: ASAP monitors 81 food-insecure countries only. A country absent from this payload is one ASAP does not watch (USA, Ukraine, Brazil, India, Australia among them) — absence must NOT be presented as an absence of stress. Unlike Aqueduct baseline and CCKP normals, this is a current-season signal and goes stale monthly; ASAP publishes around the 10th.

KGZ.comment: In Kyrgyzstan, harvest of winter wheat finalized in August while harvest of maize and spring wheat are underway, all with good prospects thanks to above average crop biomass in all regions. After a drier than average start to the season in October and especially November, moisture conditions have been conducive for cereals growth with abundant rainfall in December followed by close to average rainfall from January to June, except for a dry spell from mid March to mid April.

BGD.comment: In Bangladesh, prospects are favourable for Aman rice (35% of the country total rice production) to be harvested in November-December and Aus rice (10% of the country total rice production) whose harvest finalized in August as crop biomass is above average across the country thanks to abundant rainfall, that also caused flooding in mid July (nearly 16,000 ha of cropland were damaged in Chattogram district according to [https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01477-7/fulltext?rss=yes] the Lancet).

TJK.comment: In Tajikistan, harvest of winter and spring wheat finalized in all regions with very good prospects thanks to well above average crop biomass. After a drier than average start to the season in October November, good rainfall in December and early February and up to 8C above average temperatures in February boosted cereals growth.

SDN.comment: At roughly 30% progress of the season in Sudan's rainfed agricultural areas, rainfall deficits and above average temperatures have prevailed with exception of some areas in the south/east which are slightly better of in terms of agroecological conditions. The crop season started nearly one month late and experienced drought conditions in its early stages, making below average areas planted and weak crop conditions very likely. Seasonal forecasts from ICPAC and the Copernicus multi-model ensemble for the rest of the July-September rainy season indicate a high probability of below-average rainfall largely driven by ongoing El Niño conditions. This is further supported by ASAP seasonal forecast warnings, highlighting an elevated risk of below-average rainfall across all agricultural and pastoral areas of the country and especially in the Kordofans, White, Blue Nile and Kassala states. The negative effects on crops and rangelands caused by the rainfall deficits and heath, come on top of the livelihoods losses and degradation inflicted by the ongoing conflict, characterized by rapid movements of troops, use of drones and continuous displacement. A partially 2026 crop failure will substantially reduce the benefits of green harvest during the lean season and staples availability after harvest, contributing to extend risk of famine conditions. The main seasons of 2024 and 2025 have been characterized by generally favourable rainfall conditions. Although positive agroclimatic conditions alone were clearly not sufficient to restore rural livelihoods, they have still been supporting local crop and livestock production activities under difficult security conditions and with limited access to farming inputs. On the contrary, the 2026 dry conditions, will further worsen large-scale population displacement and compound the widespread destruction of agricultural assets, infrastructure, and basic services. After more than three years of conflict Sudan is one of the gravest food and nutrition crises globally, with 19,5 Million people affected by high levels of acute food insecurity and several areas at risk of famine as confirmed by IPC in May 2026. The [https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Sudan_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Feb2026_Jan2027_Special_Snapshot.pdf" target="_blank] IPC partial coverage special snapshot update for June–September 2026, covering 56 of Sudan's 195 localities and IDP settlements, identified a risk of famine in 14 areas across North Darfur, South Darfur, and South Kordofan under a reasonable worst-case scenario.

MOZ.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

CUB.comment: In August, the main cycle of rice should normally start the harvest while it should continue the sowing stage of the main cycle of maize and the vegetation stage of sweet potato. Rainfall in the past month has been below average, especially in the Pinar del Rio but vegetation conditions seem to be good benefitting from the excess rainfall at the beginning of the season. However, further recent sanctions targeting energy companies and further choking off fuel imports even for humanitarian purposes are leading to the energy, transport and agricultural sector, as well as basic services, complete breakdown ([https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168094] UN). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=north_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a modest probability that conditions will be direr than normal throughout the end of October.

LAO.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

DJI.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

UZB.comment: In Uzbekistan, harvest of winter cereals finalized with very good prospects as crop biomass is the highest since 2002 across all regions. After a drier than average start to the season in October and November, rainfall conditions improved and together with above average temperatures (of up to 9C in February) boosted crop growth. Harvest of maize and spring cereals is ongoing, also with good prospects.

MDG.comment: In Madagascar, apart from areas where secondary rice planting is underway, there are no cereals growing now and in the central and northern areas, the next rice season is expected to start in November with the arrival of the rainy season. In the Grand South (Anosy, Androy and Atsimo Andrefana), the next cereals season should start in October and drier than average conditions are expected in the western half of the country (including Atsimo Andrefana) according to the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast.

SLV.comment: In August, the primera crops (maize and beans) should be in the harvest stage, while rice and sorghum should continue the vegetation stage. Rainfall in the past month has been more than 40% below average which might have hindered the correct development of the crops, especially in the grain producing Eastern region. In fact, poor vegetation conditions are observed in the 26% of the Coastal region and in the 75% of the Eastern region cultivated areas. According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very direr than normal throughout the end of November, which will likely affect second cycle crops development.

MLI.comment: Over the past month, Mali experienced below-average rainfall conditions across its southern and south-central regions, while the rest of the country remained near average. The main-season maize, millet, and sorghum crops are currently in their vegetative to reproductive stages. However, below-average crop biomass conditions are visible in the Ségou, Sikasso, and Koulikoro regions, where approximately 35% to 45% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. Similarly, rangeland conditions are below average in the Sikasso and Tombouctou regions, with 25% to 30% of the active pastureland showing signs of vegetation stress. In all other regions, crop and rangeland conditions track near average. Looking forward, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 points to average conditions nationwide. Yet, despite this improved forecast for near-normal rainfall in southern Mali, the current agricultural season faces localized production deficits. These shortfalls stem from initial below-average rainfall that forced extensive replanting, compounded by persistent insecurity and limited access to critical inputs like fuel, factors that collectively reduced the country's total cultivated area by 13.2% compared to last year ([https://fews.net/west-africa/mali/key-message-update/july-2026/print] FEWS NET, July 2026).

CAF.comment: Rice (southern zones) and cassava are currently in the growth stage, with harvesting for both crops expected to begin in the last dekad of November. Precipitation over the last 30 days has been mixed across the country, with above-average rainfall in the south and below-average conditions in the north, particularly in Vakaga (-12%) and Ouham Pendé (-18%). According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/central-african-republic/republique-centrafricaine-mise-jour-sur-la-securite-alimentaire-les-resultats-de-crise-phase-3-de-lipc-persistent-dans-les-zones-enclaves-et-affectees-par-linsecurite-aout-2026-janvier-2027] FEWSNET, Crisis outcomes (IPC Phase 3) are expected to persist between August 2026 and January 2027 in the prefectures most affected by insecurity and isolation, particularly in the northeast, northwest, and Haut-Mbomou, where ongoing conflict continues to restrict access to fields, income opportunities, and key trade routes.

GHA.comment: In the southern bimodal parts of the country, the main-season maize harvest is underway with average prospects, except for the Central region where a notable drop in crop biomass was observed over the past two months. In the northern part of the country, crop conditions were below average as of mid-August; the Northern, Upper West, and Brong Ahafo regions are the most severely impacted, with approximately 30% to 45% of their active crop areas exhibiting a greenness anomaly. To a lesser extent, the Upper East region is also showing signs of vegetation stress. These localized seasonal deficits reflect broader systemic vulnerabilities. According to the [https://reliefweb.int/report/ghana/wfp-ghana-country-brief-june-2026] WFP, Ghana faces widening regional disparities, with northern and rural communities experiencing high vulnerability to climate-sensitive agricultural challenges, limited infrastructure, and food insecurity driven by global price shocks. Pasture biomass conditions across the main grazing areas of both the north and center remain stable, tracking at near-average to slightly above-average levels. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts near-average conditions nationwide, with the exception of the southern regions, which are expected to face drier-than-average conditions.

AFG.comment:
In Afghanistan, the rainfall season stopped in early June (except the eastern border e.g. Khost, Paktika, Nangarhar which receive monsoon rainfall) but biomass of spring cereals whose harvest started in August and of (irrigated) summer crops (maize harvested in August, rice to be harvested in October-November) is average to above average across the country, pointing towards favourable prospects. According to the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast, above average rainfall is expected in the coming months through December-January, in relation with the ongoing El Niño.
 Afghanistan continues to face high levels of hunger with about 14 million people estimated in acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 or above) for the period April – September 2026 as a result of prolonged economic deterioration, recurrent drought, refugee returns, declining humanitarian aid and decreasing remittances according to the latest [https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1159816/?iso3=AFG] IPC report from 16 December 2025 and [https://www.wfp.org/emergencies/afghanistan] WFP.

HTI.comment: In August, the main cycle of maize should have concluded the harvesting stage, the rice one entered the vegetation stage and the second cycle of maize concluded the sowing stage.Rainfall in the past month was below average, but despite erratic rainfall reported during the Printemps season, irrigation systems supported crop production. In fact, overall vegetation conditions seem favourable except poor conditions observed in 36% of Sud, one of the main maize producing department. According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=north_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a substantial probability that conditions will be direr than normal throughout the end of October, which might compromise water availability for the Été season maize. The security situation in the country is not improving, with recent spike in gang’s violence leading to UN Security Council emergency meeting on the 28th of August ([https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168222] UN).

TZA.comment: The Msimu crop harvest (sorghum, rice and maize) has been completed in unimodal areas, while the Masika harvest (sorghum, millet and maize) is still underway in bimodal areas. Precipitation has been average throughout the country in the last 30 days. Below average biomass conditions are present in Morogoro and Pwani, where 27% and 36% of the active crop area is seen in poor vegetation status. The current El Niño episode, hitting with dry conditions in particular the north of the country, is expected to [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] shift to wet conditions in October. In this context, Tanzania's Deputy Minister for Agriculture urged citizens on August 26 to [https://www.therespondents.co.tz/2026/08/silinde-urges-tanzanians-to-store-food.html] preserve harvested food stocks, warning that the anticipated above-average rainfall could disrupt agricultural production and heighten food insecurity risks in the coming season. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/united-republic-tanzania/wfp-tanzania-country-brief-august-2026] WFP, while agriculture remains central to livelihoods and national growth, climate shocks, rising fuel and input costs continue to pose risks to food systems and vulnerable households, reinforcing the importance of climate-smart agriculture and shock-responsive social protection.

BWA.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

IRQ.comment: In Iraq, harvest of winter wheat and barley finalized in July with good prospects except in the south due to government ban on irrigation. According to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=IRQ] FAO GIEWS, Iraq’s wheat and cereals output is forecast at 5.6 and 6.5 million tons, respectively, i.e. 34% and 31% above the respective five year averages. This year, in contrast with 2025, 2023 and 2022, rice cultivation has been authorized in the south (Najaf, Qadissiya) and rice, to be harvested in October-November, is growing under good conditions. Sowings of next season barley and wheat are expected to start in October-November under above average rainfall conditions till January, according to C3S multimodel forecast.

EGY.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

NER.comment: In Niger, during the month of August, millet and sorghum crops are predominantly in their vegetative to reproductive stages. Cumulative rainfall over the past month has been near average across most parts of the country, though localized deficits were recorded in the southwestern and south-central agricultural zones. Despite these mixed rains, overall crop and rangeland conditions remain favourable nationwide as of mid-August, with the notable exception of the Diffa region, where approximately 60% of the active crop area and 55% of the active rangeland area are affected by a greenness anomaly. According to [https://fews.net/west-africa/niger/key-message-update/july-2026/print] FEWS NET (July 2026), despite a slight decline in security incidents compared to last year, Niger's 2026 agropastoral season remains delayed; severe forage and water shortages have left livestock in poor condition across Diffa, Maradi, Zinder, and Agadez, while persistent volatility and ongoing population displacements have left over 1,300 villages unable to complete crop planting. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts average to slightly above-average conditions across the country.

MMR.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

SEN.comment: Planting of coarse grains (maize, millet, and sorghum) was finalized in July, while rice planting is expected to be completed by the end of August. Across most of the country, overall crop and pastoral biomass conditions are near average to above average due to favourable rainfall over the past month. However, localized below-average crop conditions persist in parts of central, northern, and southern Senegal. Specifically, the regions of Kaffrine, Kaolack, Matam, and Sédhiou are experiencing poor crop growth, with approximately 30% to 40% of their active crop areas affected by a greenness anomaly. These conditions are primarily attributed to early-season moisture deficits, as these areas received 45% to 60% below-average cumulative rainfall between mid-June and early July. Although precipitation has steadily improved since mid-July, the negative impact of that initial dry spell is still evident in both the agricultural fields and the pastoral zones of Kaffrine and Kaolack. In contrast, rangeland conditions throughout the rest of the country track at an average to slightly above-average level. According to the [https://reliefweb.int/report/senegal/bulletin-de-surveillance-pastorale-sur-le-senegal-ndeg47-juin-juillet-2026] Bulletin de Surveillance Pastorale sur le Sénégal N°47 (Juin – Juillet 2026), although the establishing rainy season is improving water access and pasture regeneration across Senegal, localized grazing deficits, poor livestock body conditions, high herd concentrations, and incidents of cattle theft continue to challenge herders despite otherwise favourable market prices. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 points to drier-than-average conditions concentrated along the western-central coastal area, while near-average conditions are anticipated elsewhere.

ECU.comment: In August, the second cycle of maize and the cycles of wheat and barley should enter the harvesting stage while the second rice cycle should be in the vegetation stage. Rainfall in agricultural areas has been normal in the last 30 days and vegetation conditions appear to be good, mostly in the areas of Guayas and Los Ríos, which are important grain-producing provinces.However, the Comité Nacional para el Estudio Regional del Fenómeno El Niño (CN-ERFEN) maintains the status of "El Niño Active" and recommended that the National Secretariat for Risk Management establish a Red Alert for the month of August ([https://www.inocar.mil.ec/web/index.php/boletines/erfen] ERFEN). According to the ([https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel), the probability of very wetter than normal conditions in the coastal areas is a very high through the end of the year. Conversely, in the central and western part of the country conditions are very likely to be drier than normal over the same period.

SSD.comment: Rainfall deficits have increased in the Southern part of the country over July and August and accompanied by above average temperatures. These drought conditions are showing first negative impacts in the Equatoria States (especially East Equatoria), in the central parts of the country and in Upper Nile. No impacts on vegetation are visible yet in the north/eastern part of the country. Seasonal forecasts from the ICPAC and Copernicus for the July–September period indicate a high likelihood of below-average rainfall, primarily associated with ongoing El Niño conditions. Also, independently from agro-climatic conditions, both farmers and pastoralists are highly vulnerable to the impact of conflict, economic downturn, high influx of refugees from Kordofan and internally displaced population. This scenario is further worsened by the economic effects of the conflict in Iran. An estimated 7.8 million people are experiencing IPC Phase 3 or higher (Crisis or worse) according to IPC projection update for the period from April to July 2026. This includes approximately 73,000 in IPC phase 5 (catastrophe), 2.5 million people in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) and 5.3 million in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis). According to the update, conditions have sharply worsened, with a risk of famine now identified in Luakpiny/Nasir, Ulang, Nyirol, and Akobo, driven by conflict, displacement, and restricted aid access.

MRT.comment: Planting of sorghum and maize was completed in August, following the finalization of irrigated rice planting—the country's primary cereal crop—in July. Over the past month, cumulative rainfall across the southern agricultural belt has ranged from average to above average, benefiting planting activities, germination, and early crop establishment. Consequently, both crop and rangeland conditions were favourable across these southern zones as of mid-August. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts a continuation of near-average conditions across this same agricultural belt.

AGO.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

NIC.comment:
In August, the primera crops maize, beans and sorghum are normally in the harvest stage while land preparation activities are ongoing for the postrera (second cycle). Both seasons are affected by the El Nino induced drier than normal conditions, particularly in the areas of the dry corridor. 
The past three months rainfall was almost a third below average, resulting in poor vegetation conditions across more than 47% of the country. Most affected areas are the departments of Chinandega, Leon, Managua and Matagalpa, where poor vegetation conditions are observed in large part of the cropping areas.Contrarily to other countries in the region, agricultural activities are not significantly affected by the energy price spikes as the Government of Nicaragua imposed a freeze on fuel and butane gas prices since 2022, absorbing the price fluctuations due to the energy crisis ([https://repositorio.cepal.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/5ba9f6d5-ccf1-4cdb-a8a0-2f0159a62548/content] ECLAC). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, the situation is not expected to improve as drier that normal conditions are expected across the country until the end of October.

ERI.comment: Crop areas in Gash Barka and Debub continued to experienced heat and below average rainfall in August. ASAP forecast warnings predict negative vegetation anomalies for the rest of the main season, making significant recovery unlikely. Coastal rangeland areas might benefit from above average rainfall in October/December according to seasonal weather forecasts.

HND.comment: In August, the primera cycle of maize and beans should have entered the harvesting stage, while the main sorghum and rice cycles should have entered the vegetation stage. The postrera cycle of maize and beans should start in this month. The primera season has experienced below average rainfall since the onset, leading to poor crop conditions in most cropping areas. The Secretary of State in the Offices of Risk Management and National Contingencies (COPECO), declared a Red Alert for 103 municipalities due to drought associated with the El Niño phenomenon, located in the departments of Choluteca, Comayagua, El Paraíso, Francisco Morazán, La Paz and Valle ([https://copeco.gob.hn/] COPECO). Around 1 million people are being directly affected by the drought ([https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-drought-assessment-2026-dref-operation-mdrhn028] IFRC).In addition, the country is among the hardest hit by the increase in price of fuel, with around +60% year on year change. Prospects are not favourable for the entire second cycle of crops as, according to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the country until the end of November.

DZA.comment:
In Algeria, harvest of winter cereals finalized in mid-August with very good prospects: wheat and barley productions are estimated at 3.5 and 1.3 million tons respectively by [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=DZA] FAO GIEWS, up by +28% and +40% with respect their five-year average. The FAO GIEWS forecast of 4.9 million tons of cereals (+30% with respect to the 5-year average) is close to the “historical” cereals harvest of 5 million tons (+33%) announced by the [https://www.tsa-algerie.com/cereales-lalgerie-sattend-a-une-recolte-record-de-5-millions-de-tonnes/] ministry of agriculture, and above [https://algerie-eco.com/2026/08/17/production-agricole-en-algerie-ce-que-dit-lusda/] USDA reported forecast 
of 4.65 million tons of cereals (+23%). Clearly, the output 2026 is above average and created a logistical [https://www.tsa-algerie.com/recolte-exceptionnelle-de-cereales-lalgerie-decrete-la-grande-mobilisation/] stress on combine harvesters. Sowings of next season cereals are expected to start in October, with favourable rainfall conditions till October followed by drier than average conditions from November to January according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.

BOL.comment: In August, wheat, the main cycle of sorghum and the minor cycle of maize normally finish the harvest stage. Main areas cultivated are concentrated in the main grain producing department of Santa Cruz, where rainfall were normal to above normal in the past months and vegetation conditions seem good. Nonetheless, the country is the hardest hit in the region by the increase in price of fuel, with more than 87% increase in the price of gasoline and 165% in the price of diesel compared to the year before mostly due to the end of the 15-year U.S. dollar peg in July ([https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/bolivia-ends-15-year-dollar-peg-attempt-restore-economic-stability-2026-06-27/] Reuters). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel, there is a high probability of wetter than normal conditions persisting through September but becoming drier than normal in the following months in the central and western part of the country.

ZMB.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

CIV.comment: The main-season maize harvest is currently underway in the southern bimodal parts of the country, with average prospects supported by generally favourable rains throughout the season. Planting of the secondary maize crop, predominantly cultivated in the south, is ongoing and will be completed in September. In the North, which only has one rainy season, planting of the 2026 coarse grains was recently finalized, with harvesting expected to begin in October. Crop conditions are below-average in the northern regions of Savanes, Denguélé, and Bandama, where approximately 30% of the active crop area is showing signs of a greenness anomaly. The poor crop conditions are primarily attributed to the ongoing security and humanitarian crises in the Central Sahel, which continue to spill over into northern Côte d’Ivoire. Persistent regional instability is driving an influx of refugees into these northern areas, restricting access to both farmland and grazing areas ([https://fews.net/west-africa/cote-divoire/key-message-update/july-2026/print] FEWS NET, [https://reliefweb.int/report/cote-divoire/wfp-cote-divoire-country-brief-july-2026] WFP, [https://reliefweb.int/report/cote-divoire/cote-divoire-factsheet-january-june-2026] UNHCR). Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts drier-than-average conditions across central and southern regions, while the rest of the country is expected to receive near-average rainfall.

GTM.comment: In August, the primera cycle of maize should have finalised the vegetation stage while rice starts the harvest. Postrera crops should start the sowing stage.Rainfall in the past three months has been erratic and below average throughout the country and mostly in the Dry Corridor areas, leading to planting delays and poor crop conditions. The worst affected areas by the El Niño-driven dry conditions and the higher-than-average temperatures are Montagua Valley, Central and Eastern regions and Verapaz. In addition, the country is among the hardest hit by the increase in price of fuel, with around +35% year on year change. According to the International Phase Classification, in Guatemala more than 3.2 million people, 17% of the population of the country is projected to face Crisis level food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) with 197 000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) between July and September 2026 ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165394/?iso3=GTM] IPC).

TGO.comment: Cumulative rainfall over the last three months has been generally average to slightly above-average across the country. Harvesting of the main season maize crop in southern parts of the country is underway and an average output is expected. In the north, which only has one rainy season, cereals are in the growing stage. Below-average vegetation conditions are observed in the northern regions of Savanes and Kara. A greenness anomaly affects roughly 30% to 40% of the active crop area and around 30% of the active rangeland area in the two regions. These poor crop conditions stem from severe early-season dry spells and compounded by escalating localized conflict. The persistent risks of armed incursions and extremist infiltration along the northern borders have severely constrained agricultural access, economic activity, and trade—further weakening household livelihoods and food consumption—while driving the displacement of 13,400 IDPs and the arrival of 65,100 refugees and asylum-seekers into Togo from the Central Sahel as of June 2026 ([https://reliefweb.int/report/togo/togo-factsheet-january-june-2026] UNHCR, [https://fews.net/fr/west-africa/togo/mise-jour-des-messages-cles/juillet-2026/print] FEWS NET (July 2026)). Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts average conditions across the country except for the southern part where drier-than-average conditions are forecast.

MAR.comment: In Morocco, harvest of winter cereals finalized in June with excellent prospects, as suggested by well above average crop biomass. Actually, in mid-June the ministry of agriculture announced a [https://fr.le360.ma/economie/agriculture-ahmed-el-bouari-confirme-une-recolte-cerealiere-record-de-90-millions-de-quintaux_EF7FDH57IZFJTE6TTSDKPY6ISY/] record harvest with winter wheat and barley productions estimated at 6.5 and 2.5 million tons respectively (more precisely 4.4 and 2.1 million tons for soft wheat and durum wheat respectively), i.e. 60% and 94% above the respective 2021-2025 average wheat and barley productions. These estimations are much higher than the early July [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=MAR] forecasts of FAO GIEWS (5 M t for wheat and 1.2 M t for barley, i.e. +23% and -7% of the respective five year average productions), and are closer to the [https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/gain/2026/04/morocco-grain-and-feed-annual] USDA wheat forecast of mid-April (4.2, 2.3 and 1.5 million t for soft wheat, durum wheat and barley respectively, i.e. 60% and 17% above the five year average productions of wheat and barley) . After four years of below average output due to low rainfall, this very good harvest is welcome. Sowings of next season cereals are expected to take place in November-December, under average to below average rainfall conditions according to the C3S multimodel forecast.

TUN.comment: In Tunisia, harvest of winter barley and wheat finalized in June with good prospects. According to the [https://www.lapresse.tn/2026/08/01/recolte-cerealiere-plus-de-107-millions-de-quintaux-collectes/] ministry of agriculture, 2 million tons of cereals have been harvested (35% above the five-year average), a higher estimate than the [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=TUN] FAO GIEWS forecast of 1.8 million tons of cereals (+20%, distributed mainly in 1.2 million tons of wheat and 0.55 t of barley). Sowings of next season cereals are expected to start in October. Rainfall is expected above average till October and below average from November to January according to C3S multimodel forecast.

TKM.comment: In Turkmenistan, harvest of winter cereals finalized in August while harvest of spring cereals is underway, both with very good prospects as crop biomass is well above average in all regions. Winter cereals benefitted from average to above average rainfall since December and average to above average temperatures since October, in particular in February where temperatures reached 8C above normal.

PHL.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

IRN.comment: In Iran, harvest of winter wheat finalized in July with average to above average prospects across the country except in few provinces of the centre (Tehran, Markazi and Esfahan). According to [https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/1c2612f4-2392-4938-8dd6-064c61d1528f/content] FAO crop prospects and food situation report, Iran’s cereals output is forecast at 21.6 million tons, close to its five-year average (21.4 million tons) and up by 11% with respect to the 19.5 million tons produced in 2025, thanks to good rainfall from December to May. As for rice production, harvest is underway in the north (Gilan, Mazandaran and Golestan which makes up 70% of the national production) and crop biomass suggests average to above average prospects in the north as well as in Khuzestan but not in Fars. According to Eqtesad-e Moaser (quoted in FAO crop prospects and food situation report), rice production is forecast at 3.9 million tons, as in 2025, which is 8% above the 2021-2025 average.

NAM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

GMB.comment: Millet, rice, and maize crops are in their growing stages during August, supported by slightly above-average cumulative rainfall over the past month that has benefited both crop development and pasture regeneration. Consequently, crop and rangeland biomass conditions remain near average nationwide as of mid-August. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts near-average conditions across most of the country, with the exception of the western region, which is expected to experience drier-than-average conditions.

KHM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

LSO.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

VNM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

CMR.comment: The harvest of main-season maize in the bimodal central and southern parts of the country began in mid-August. Crop conditions in these areas have generally benefited from a timely onset of the rainy season and good seasonal rainfall amounts. In the north, harvesting is expected to begin in late September. While crop conditions there were close to average as of mid-August, reduced yields are expected in some areas. More specifically, below-average crop conditions are visible in the Nord region, where almost 35% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. Conversely, rangeland conditions across the country were average to slightly above average as of mid-August and are expected to adequately support livestock production. However, structural challenges persist; according to [https://fews.net/west-africa/cameroon/key-message-update/july-2026/print] FEWS NET (July 2026), agricultural production prospects in conflict-affected areas of the northern zone remain below average. This downturn is driven by persistent insecurity, diminished humanitarian aid, and a 30 to 40 percent spike in fertilizer prices, all of which have severely restricted poor households' farming activities and access to critical inputs.

LKA.comment: In Sri Lanka, harvest of second season (Yala) rice and maize is underway with good prospects thanks to above average crop biomass in the main producing provinces.

ZAF.comment: Winter wheat biomass conditions are favourable in the Cape area. However, according to the [https://www.sagis.org.za/crop-estimates-committee-2/" rel="noreferrer noopener" target="_blank" title="https://www.sagis.org.za/crop-estimates-committee-2/] 1st production forecast, total winter wheat production is expected below the 5-year average, at 1,762 million tons.

COG.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

MWI.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

BDI.comment: Most of the country is currently in the off-season, with Season B crops including beans, sorghum, and maize fully harvested. Yield prospects are at or slightly below average, reflecting poor rainfall performance throughout the season linked to the persisting El Niño episode. Above-average temperatures have been recorded across the country over the last three dekads, with peaks reaching +7% above the long-term average in Gitega. [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service indicate above-average rainfall in Burundi during the OND rainy season. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/burundi/wfp-burundi-country-brief-august-2026] WFP, the 2026 Season B harvest brought continued seasonal relief, improving food availability compared to June, with 66 percent of key informants reporting increased stocks. However, supplies remain below July 2025 levels due to drought in the north and flooding in the west, with most staple food prices still above their five-year average reflecting structural market pressures.

NGA.comment: Over the last three months, cumulative rainfall across Nigeria has been mixed, remaining average across most central regions, slightly above average in the east, and below average in both the northwest and parts of the far southern coast. In the southern bimodal areas, the main-season maize harvest is currently underway, with average production prospects thanks to average biomass conditions as of mid-August. Meanwhile, in north, which has only one rainy season, the harvesting of coarse grains is set to begin in September, supported by average to above-average vegetation conditions. In contrast, vegetation anomalies are observed across the Middle Belt states, specifically Niger, Plateau, Nassarawa, and Kwara, where approximately 35% to 60% of the active crop area is experiencing a greenness deficit. Below-average crop biomass conditions are also observed in the northeast (Adamawa and Bauchi states) and the northwest (Kaduna state). Similarly, poor pastoral conditions are impacting the same zones, leaving nearly 30% of active rangeland nationwide affected by a greenness anomaly, according to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/country.php?cntry=182] ASAP Country page. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 projects average rainfall in northern Nigeria but predicts drier, below-average conditions across the southern and central regions. According to [https://fews.net/west-africa/nigeria/key-message-update/july-2026/print] FEWS NET (July 2026), agricultural activities are severely impeded by ongoing armed conflict, rising fuel and input costs, and public health crises that deplete farming labor and financial resources. Together, these compounding climate, economic, and security factors continue to challenge food production and overall food security.

SOM.comment: The Gu seasons has ended for the rainfed areas in Somalia and has been characterized by a delayed onset, erratic rainfall distribution and high temperatures, causing drought conditions in parts of the south and central parts of the country since May 2026. These conditions are likely to have caused crop failures in parts of Bay, Lower Shabelle, Middle Juba and Hiraan states. In a similar way pastoral vegetation was strongly depleted in most of southern and central Somalia by the end of July. According to satellite imagery, the high potential sorghum areas in the northern part of the Bay region and in riverine areas experienced close to average vegetation conditions, but it is difficult to draw conclusions on final yields without ground information. Overall, there are high concerns that a partial 2026 Gu harvest failure has taken place and risks to compound the severe impacts of the 2025 Deyr drought, during which large parts of the country experienced crop failure or significantly below-average yields, alongside reduced livestock production. Floods in September/October are likely with the current El Niño conditions and might cause further negative impacts on livelihoods. At the same time, Somalia remains highly dependent on imported food and fuel from the Gulf region, leaving it vulnerable to regional supply disruptions and price shocks. According to [https://fews.net/east-africa/somalia" target="_blank] FEWSNET, food assistance needs are expected to be extremely high until January 2027 and a risk of famine had been predicted since June in parts of Bay Region.

COD.comment: The harvest of maize (second season), rice (north), cassava (south), and yams has been completed, while the planting of maize (center/main season) and cassava (south) is underway. Precipitation in the last 30 days has been mostly average throughout the DRC, except in the northeast. In Ituri and North Kivu, rainfall has been -40% and -17% compared to the long-term average. Below-average biomass conditions at the start of the season are recorded in Kwilu, where 60% of the active agricultural area is in poor vegetation status. Similar conditions are present in Kwango and Kasai, due to poor soil moisture resulting from rainfall underperformance in the last 90 days. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/democratic-republic-congo/republique-democratique-du-congo-mise-jour-sur-la-securite-alimentaire-la-poursuite-des-violences-presage-une-soudure-precoce-pour-les-menages-aout-2026-janvier-2027] FEWSNET, Crisis outcomes (IPC Phase 3) are expected to persist through January 2027 in the eastern part of the country, driven by ongoing conflict disrupting livelihoods, markets, and trade.

LBR.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

PRK.comment: In DPRK, maize harvest has started while rice should be harvested in September-October and for both crops prospects are favourable as crop biomass is above average in all provinces thanks to abundant rainfall, especially in July. Actually the whole peninsula received abundant rainfall, especially the south of the rice bowl area (South and North Hwanghae) where July rainfall was 3 to 4 times the usual rainfall (1150 to 1300 mm versus an average amount of 300 to 350 mm), which probably resulted in flooding. Indeed, flooding has been reported by [https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/north-korea-says-thousands-homes-hit-by-flooding-2024-07-30/] Reuters in North Pyongan (3000 ha of farmland flooded in Sinuiju city and Yuiju county, close to the border with China) and by [https://www.nknews.org/pro/flooding-wipes-out-north-korean-villages-at-key-military-base-near-border/] NK Pro in the Singye county, North Hwanghae, close to the south Korean border, but no thorough assessment of flooded farmland was published.

KEN.comment: Vegetation conditions in the north/eastern parts of Kenya deteriorated further in August, reflecting a rapid deterioration of pastoral vegetation in the ASALs. This is due to cumulative effects of below-average rainfall since late May and throughout June and July as well as above average temperatures. In the unimodal cropping zones, below-average rainfall slowed crop development and reduced soil moisture availability during critical crop growth stages causing clearly below average crop production expectations both in Western Kenya and in the Rift Valley counties, Kenya's main bread basket. Looking ahead, forecasts of a strong El Niño for the upcoming short rains season point to above average rainfall. It is important however to bear in mind that high intensity rainfall will not be immediately beneficial to drought affected crop areas and that there is a high risk of adverse impacts including increased risk of flooding. These conditions could further affect agricultural production, disrupt livelihoods, and complicate recovery efforts in areas already impacted by the current dry spell.

YEM.comment: In Yemen, sowings of sorghum and millet just completed in the Coastal Areas while both crops are in vegetative to reproductive stage in the Northern & Central Highlands and Southern Uplands. The second rain season (Kharif) started in early July with 30 to 60% rainfall deficit but rainfall improved at end of July and has been close to average in the last month, resulting in close to average crop biomass. Food insecurity remains high with about 17 million food insecure people out of 40 million people according to [https://www.wfp.org/countries/yemen] WFP, mainly as a result of the socio economic conditions and conflict.

TLS.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

SLE.comment: The planting of minor coarse grains (sorghum. millet, maize) finalized in June (for sorghum) and July (for millet, maize). Planting of rice, the main cereal grown in the country, was completed at the end of July. Crop conditions are close to average across the country, however water stressed vegetation conditions are visible in the Northern province. Pastoral conditions remain at a good level as of mid-August. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts drier-than-average conditions across the western and southern part of the country and near-average across the northeastern part.

LBY.comment: In Libya, harvest of barley and wheat finalized in May and June respectively with mixed prospects, i.e. poor in the Tripoli area going from Az Zawia to Misurata, most likely due to a reduction of the sown area, and good around Banghazi (e.g. in Al Fatah) except in Darnah. According to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=LBY] FAO GIEWS, the 2026 harvest of cereals (wheat and barley mainly) is forecast at about 150,000 tons, i.e. 20% below the five year average.

RWA.comment: Most of the country is currently in the off-season as season B crops including beans, sorghum, and maize have been fully harvested. Yield prospects are below average due to poor rainfall performance throughout the season, linked to the persisting El Niño episode. Average temperature has been recorded above average throughout the country during the last three dekads, with peaks of +11% against the long-term average in Nyagatare. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/rwanda/wfp-rwanda-country-brief-august-2026] WFP, recent harvests have nonetheless improved the availability of staple foods, contributing to stable food basket costs and price reductions, particularly in more productive regions. Looking ahead, Rwanda is forecast to receive above-average rainfall during the OND rainy season, as pointed by the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service.

GNB.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

IDN.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

ETH.comment: During the vegetative stadium of the main crop season in Ethiopia (Meher), vegetation conditions from satellite show below average conditions in most of Ethiopia, with strong impact visible in crop and rangeland areas in Tigray, in the Rift Valley and Harerge areas, extending southwards into Bale, Arsi and Omo areas. Rainfall deficits in the initial part of the Meher season have continued in the north, Rift Valley and south of the country, coupled with above average temperature and heatwaves in July and in August. Crop conditions in these areas are not at the level of crop failure but will most likely drive low yields. Biomass conditions in the highlands of the western part of the country seem less negatively affected according to satellite imagery. Seasonal rainfall forecasts continue to point towards below average rainfall in the north of the country from September to January, whereas a wetter than normal season is expected in the southern Deyr areas, which might benefit rangeland areas in Southern Ethiopia. Despite a favourable Belg season in the first part of 2026, concerns over the food security outlook situation are rapidly increasing, driven by the below average early Meher season conditions and by rapidly increasing food and fuel prices during the lean season, which continue to erode household purchasing power.

KAZ.comment: In Kazakhstan, harvest of winter wheat (which represents 5% of the total wheat production) finalized in the southern regions with close to average prospects while harvest of spring wheat and barley (which account for 95% of cereals output) are underway in the main producing regions of the north (Severo, Kustanayskaia and Akmolinskaya) with very good prospects as favourable rainfall and above average temperature conditions resulted in well above average biomass (crop biomass is below average only in minor producing regions in the centre of the country, namely Karagandingskaia, Vostochno).

THA.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

NPL.comment: In Nepal, rice planting finalized in August under favourable moisture conditions while maize harvest started with favourable prospects, as suggested by above average crop biomass in all provinces.

COL.comment: In August, main cycles of rice, the minor of maize, sorghum, barley and wheat are normally in the harvesting stage. The main cycle of maize usually starts at the end of this month. Cumulative rainfall of the past three months has been below average with poor vegetation conditions shown across cropping areas, particularly in the rice-producing areas of Cauca, Huila and Tolima, where 26%, 43% and 46% of their respective agricultural areas exhibit poor vegetation health. On the 10th of August, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, leaving an estimated 1.2 million people need humanitarian assistance. As it coincided with key crop planting and harvesting seasons, the disruption threatens to break production cycles for rural and family farming communities ([https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168178] UN).Contrary to other countries in the region, the fluctuations of fuel price are in large part absorbed by the Fondo de Estabilización de Precios de los Combustibles (FEPC), which declared to freeze the price due to the earthquake emergency. According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel, there is a high probability of very drier than normal conditions persisting through November throughout the country, likely to affect the next cycle of maize and a correct development of crops.

GIN.comment: Planting of coarse grains crops (maize, millet and sorghum) was completed in June, while planting operations of rice, the most important crop produced in the country, are about to conclude. As of mid-August, crop and rangeland conditions are good across the country, except for the eastern regions of Kankan and Nzérékoré, where approximately 30% to 40% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 points to average conditions across the country.

BEN.comment: The first-season maize harvest is currently underway in the southern parts of the country, with average prospects supported by generally favourable, near-average cumulative rainfall during crop development. Conversely, well below-average crop biomass conditions are observed in the northern unimodal areas, where the planting of coarse grains and rice was finalized in July. More specifically, in Borgou province, close to 75% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. The provinces of Alibori, Atakora, and Donga are also impacted, albeit to a lesser extent, with approximately 40% to 50% of their active crop areas showing signs of vegetation stress. Rangeland conditions are similarly poor across these northern departments; Borgou is the most severely affected, with around 70% of its rangeland area compromised, followed by Alibori, Atakora, and Donga at 30% to 40%. Persistent insecurity appears to be a key driver of these poor crop and rangeland conditions in the north. According to the [https://reliefweb.int/report/benin/wfp-benin-country-brief-august-2026] WFP (Benin Country Brief, August 2026), the resurgence of armed incidents linked to the Sahel crisis continues to worsen the humanitarian situation in Benin, particularly in the Atacora, Alibori, and Borgou departments, which are hosting internally displaced persons alongside refugees and asylum seekers from Burkina Faso, Niger, Togo, and Nigeria. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 points to average conditions across most parts of the country, except for the southern region, where drier-than-average conditions are expected.

GNQ.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

PAK.comment: In Pakistan, conditions of Kharif maize and rice to be harvested as from mid-September are mixed, i.e. above average in Punjab and below average in Sindh and Balochistan, probably as a result of the delayed start of the monsoon in the south (the monsoon started around end July instead of end June in Sindh and Balochistan) and despite the availability of irrigation water in the Tabella and Mangla dams in the north, which are now at or close to their maximum capacity according to the [https://www.facebook.com/reel/3375298835975981] Pakistan Meteorological Department. According to the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast, rainfall is expected below average for September, which corresponds to the end of the monsoon season, and above average for October – December when most of rice and maize harvest takes place as well as sowings of Rabi crops (wheat and barley).

PER.comment: In August, all major food crops should be in the harvesting stage except sorghum, which should be finalizing the sowing phase, and yellow maize, which is starting a new cycle. Rainfall in the past month has been normal throughout the country except for the coastal area, where it was above average. Large areas of croplands in Arequipa, important grain-producing department, present poor vegetation conditions likely linked to heavy rains, floods and landslides the area suffered earlier in the year. In August, the Comisión Multisectorial encargada del Estudio Nacional del Fenómeno "El Niño" maintains an active "Alerta de El Niño Costero", with high probability that the phenomenon persists until summer 2027 ([https://enfen.imarpe.gob.pe/" style="font-family: Verdana; font-style: normal; background-color: rgb(255, 255, 255);] ENFEN).In addition, the country is among the hardest hit in the region by the increase in price of fuel, with up to +68% year on year change. According to the ([https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel), the probability of wetter than normal conditions in the coastal areas is a very high through the end of the year. Conversely, in the central and western part of the country conditions are very likely to be normal to drier than normal over the same period.

UGA.comment: Poor and inconsistent rainfall from June to August together with high temperatures prevailed in the unimodal areas of Karamoja pointing to low harvest expectations. Similar conditions but in a more patchy patter are also visible in the eastern and central parts of the country and might locally hamper planting of second season crops in the bimodal areas. According to [https://fews.net/east-africa/uganda" target="_blank] FEWSNET the increased refugee numbers in Karamoja, together with the poor harvest and high food prices contributes to rapidly increasing humanitarian needs. Patches of worsening vegetation conditions shown by satellite imagery in the east and central parts of the country also point towards decreasing rangeland availability for livestock.

SWZ.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

TCD.comment: Rainfall performance has been highly irregular across Chad, characterized by severe precipitation deficits and high temperatures at the start of the 2026 agricultural season in May, followed by near-average conditions in June, and a return to below-average rainfall and elevated temperatures over the past month. Consequently, both cropland and rangeland biomass conditions remain below-average across most parts of the country. At the national level, approximately 45% of the active crop area and more than 30% of the active rangeland area are affected by a negative greenness anomaly. The most severely impacted areas include the Sudanian regions of Logone Occidental, Logone Oriental, Tandjilé, Mayo-Kebbi Ouest, Mandoul, and Mayo-Kebbi Est, alongside the Sahelian regions of Ouaddaï, Batha and Sila. Compounding these environmental stressors, persistent insecurity remains a primary driver of food insecurity; according to [https://fews.net/west-africa/chad/key-message-update/july-2026/print] FEWS NET (July 2026), escalating Boko Haram attacks in Lac Province and clashes surrounding refugee disarmament and water access in eastern provinces like Wadi Fira and Ouaddaï continue to create a climate of fear that drives population displacement and severely disrupts local livelihoods. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts near-average conditions nationwide, with the exception of the southern and southeastern regions, which are expected to face drier-than-average conditions.

ZWE.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

BFA.comment: Development of main-season sorghum, maize, and millet is currently underway, though overall conditions remain mixed. Poor rainfall throughout July, combined with irregular precipitation during the first two dekads of August, has resulted in below-average biomass conditions across many parts of the country. Specifically, the central regions of Centre-Ouest, Plateau-Central, and Centre exhibit poor crop biomass across 45% to 65% of their active cropland. A similar downward trend is visible in the west (Boucle du Mouhoun and Hauts-Bassins) and the southeast (Centre-Est), where approximately 30% to 40% of the active crop area is experiencing poor biomass development. Furthermore, below-average crop conditions are observed in the north-central, south-central, far northern, and far southwestern zones. As of mid-August, the Sahel and Est regions are the only areas where crop conditions track at near-average to above-average levels. Pastoral conditions remain average across most of the country except for the central regions, where poor biomass development is evident. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_08_2-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for September 2026 predicts average conditions nationwide; if this favorable outlook materializes, it could potentially offset the delayed crop growth observed in mid-August.

SYR.comment: In Syria, harvest of wheat and barley finalized in August with very good prospects, after a drier than average start of season in the northwestern governorates. According to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=SYR] FAO GIEWS, the 2026 harvest of cereals is forecast at about 4.6 million tons (2.7 million t for wheat and 1.6 million t for barley mainly), i.e. 70% above the five year average (+56% and +184% for wheat and barley respectively) and 3.7 times the 2025 very poor cereals output.Sowings of next season cereals are expected to start in October under above average rainfall conditions till November and close to average conditions in December and January, according to C3S multimodel forecast. Food insecurity remains high with about 6 million people in need of food assistance (for a total population of 24 million) according to [https://fews.net/middle-east-and-europe/syria/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWSNET Junereport, mainly as a result of the economic situation, which affects especially poor households and IDPs (despite favourable weather conditions) and reduction in humanitarian assistance in 2026.
